The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan: The School of Narbonne and the Shaping of Midrash in Provence
This article surveys the life and intellectual contribution of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan, one of the prominent sages of Narbonne in the 11th century, who served as a vital link between the ancient traditions of midrash and European biblical exegesis. The text highlights his distinctive exegetical method, which combines extensive use of gematriot and allusions with a rare preservation of lost external sources such as the Book of Enoch and Jubilees. Beyond his role as head of a yeshiva and spiritual leader, the article underscores his decisive influence on Rashi's commentary on Scripture, which regarded his work "Sefer Yesod" as a central authoritative source. Finally, the source discusses the scholarly vicissitudes of the midrash "Bereshit Rabbati" and the sage's messianic and cosmological conceptions, which shape to this day our understanding of the development of midrashic literature in the Middle Ages.
The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan: The School of Narbonne and the Shaping of Midrash in Provence
The 11th century in southern France, and especially in the city of Narbonne, marked the beginning of a decisive period in the history of rabbinic literature. At the center of this transition stands the figure of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan, a sage who served as a link between the ancient traditions of midrash and the developing European exegesis, and whose influence on the great Rishonim, foremost among them Rashi, was unprecedented.[1, 2] The figure of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan is not confined to the role of a biblical commentator alone, but encompasses that of a head of a yeshiva, an editor of midrashim, and the author of a distinctive exegetical method that incorporates elements of gematria, the use of forgotten external literature and complex cosmological conceptions.[2, 3]
The Historical and Biographical Background: The Dynasty of the Sages of Narbonne
Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan was active in the first half of the 11th century in Narbonne in the region of Provence (known also as the Provincia). At that time Narbonne was a central Torah center, and its Jewish community enjoyed spiritual autonomy and a rich tradition of learning.[2, 3] According to the historical sources, foremost among them "Sefer ha-Yuchasin" by Rabbi Avraham Zacut, Rabbi Moshe was a scion of a distinguished family of Torah scholars who held the leadership of the yeshiva in the city for generations.[3]
The structure of the family dynasty and the leadership of the yeshiva in Narbonne attest to the stability of the Torah center in which he grew up:
The Dynasty of the Heads of the Yeshiva in Narbonne
As head of the yeshiva, Rabbi Moshe engaged not only in homiletics but also in halakha and Talmud, as attested by the fact that his foremost disciple, Rabbi Nathan of Rome, author of the "Arukh," quotes him several times in linguistic and talmudic contexts.[1, 2] The yeshiva in Narbonne under his leadership was a magnet for many students, and it was this yeshiva that shaped the intellectual foundation on which Provençal and French exegesis was later built.[2]
His Literary Work: "Sefer Yesod" and Its Influence on Rashi
Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan's principal work was known as "Sefer Yesod" (The Book of Foundation) or simply "the Yesod of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan."[1] This book was not a classic biblical commentary, but a wide-ranging anthology of ancient midrashim, which Rabbi Moshe collected and arranged in the order of the verses of the Torah, incorporating his own original comments and homilies.[1, 2]
The importance of "Sefer Yesod" for the history of biblical exegesis is immense, chiefly owing to the fact that Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki) regarded it as an authoritative and central source. Rashi uses explicit expressions to indicate his debt to Rabbi Moshe, such as "I found in the Yesod of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan," "I learned it from the words of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan" or "I copied from the Yesod of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan."[1, 3] The extent of Rashi's quotations from Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan shows that Rashi saw him as the foremost representative of the midrashic tradition, one that makes it possible to interpret Scripture in a way that combines the depth of derash with the need to resolve difficulties in the text.[1, 2]
Although the original "Sefer Yesod" has not survived in our hands as a complete work, its citations are scattered not only in Rashi's commentary but also in the writings of the Tosafists (for example, in tractate Sotah 36b) and in later works such as "Pa'aneach Raza."[1] The disappearance of the complete book is considered one of the great losses of medieval literature, but the influence of the work remains engraved in the heart of the Jewish exegetical canon.[2]
The Midrash "Bereshit Rabbati": Formation and Rediscovery
One of the works most identified with the figure of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan in the modern era is the midrash "Bereshit Rabbati." Modern scholarship regards this work as an abridgment or adaptation of the material that appeared in "Sefer Yesod" on the Book of Genesis.[4, 5] The midrash is characterized by its broad scope (hence its name "Rabbati," "the great") and by its use of diverse sources, ranging from the classical midrashim of the Sages to external literature.[5, 6]
The History of the Manuscript and Its Study
The discovery and publication of "Bereshit Rabbati" involve a detective story of historical research. In the 13th century, the Dominican friar Raymundus Martini quoted in his anti-Jewish book "Pugio Fidei" (The Dagger of Faith) from a work he called "Bereshit Rabbah of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan."[1, 4] Since the original book was not known to Jewish sages at that time, Rabbi Yitzhak Abravanel suspected that Martini had forged the quotations in order to support Christian claims.[4]
Only in the 19th century did Rabbi Shlomo Yehuda Rapoport (Shir) locate a manuscript of the midrash in Prague.[4] This discovery led to a scholarly controversy over whether this was indeed the original book of Rabbi Moshe:
Shlomo Yehuda Rapoport (Shir): identified the manuscript as the work of Rabbi Moshe.[4]
Yom-Tov Lipmann Zunz and Avraham Epstein: supported the attribution to Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan after finding many parallels between the manuscript and the quotations of Martini and Rashi.[4]
Shlomo Buber: doubted the direct attribution, arguing that some of the famous citations of Rabbi Moshe are missing from the manuscript.[4]
Chanoch Albeck: concluded in his study of 1940 that the manuscript is an authoritative abridgment from the school of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan, and published it in a scholarly edition.[4, 5]
The manuscript used by Albeck (Vatican 30) is considered an excellent text consisting of 101 sections, sometimes organized according to the division of the portions of the triennial reading cycle that was customary in the Land of Israel.[6]
Exegetical Methodology: Gematria, Allusions and Secrets
The uniqueness of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan lies in his exegetical method, which departs from the accepted rules of tannaitic and amoraic midrash. He developed a language of "allusions" that seeks to uncover hidden layers in the biblical text by means of mathematical tools and combinations of letters.[2, 3]
The Use of Gematria
Gematria in the work of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan is not merely a homiletic ornament, but an essential tool of decoding. A prominent example attributed to him in Rashi's commentary is the homily on the words "I have sojourned with Laban" (Genesis 32:5). Rabbi Moshe notes that the word "garti" (I have sojourned) in gematria is 613 (taryag), an allusion to the fact that Jacob observed all the commandments in the house of Laban.[7]
Further examples of his method include:
The calculation of Eliezer: the identification of Abraham's 318 trained men with Eliezer alone (Eliezer = 318).[7]
Nazirite vow: deriving the duration of the Nazirite vow (30 days) from the word "yihyeh" (shall be) (in gematria 30) in the verse "he shall be holy."[7]
In the Scroll of Esther: the phrase "the silver is given to you" (ha-kesef = 165 = ha-etz, "the tree"), an allusion to the hanging of Haman.[7]
This method of using gematriot and allusions greatly influenced later commentators, foremost among them Rabbi Yaakov ben Asher (the "Baal ha-Turim"), who made gematria an inseparable part of his commentary on the Torah.[7]
Integration of Sources and Editorial Style
Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan used to cite in his works passages from other midrashim, sometimes with a change of wording or in abridged form, in order to fit them to the structure of his commentary.[2] He used midrashim some of which were almost lost, such as "Midrash Tadshe" (also called "Baraita de-Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair") and the Midrash of the Ten Commandments.[1, 2] His skill as a compiler made it possible to create a rich exegetical fabric that combines halakha and aggadah in a synthetic manner.[2]
The Bridge to the External Literature: Enoch and the Book of Jubilees
One of the most astonishing features of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan's teaching, fully revealed only in modern scholarship, is his extensive use of external books from the Second Temple period.[3, 5, 8] These are works such as 1 Enoch and the Book of Jubilees, which almost vanished from the rabbinic Jewish tradition and were preserved mainly in Christian communities (such as the Ethiopian Church).[8]
Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan apparently knew Hebrew versions of these books that have not come down to us today.[3] This integration gives his midrashim a distinctive character:
The Book of Jubilees: Rabbi Moshe uses the biographical and chronological details that appear in this book to supplement the stories of the patriarchs in Genesis, details that do not appear in Scripture or in the classical midrashim of the Sages.[5, 8]
The Book of Enoch and the fall of the angels: "Bereshit Rabbati" contains a detailed description of the story of the angels Shemchazai and Aza'el, their descent to earth and their sin with the daughters of men (according to Genesis 6:2).[9] The description includes the teaching of the "Explicit Name" to a woman named Estirah, and the birth of the giants (the "Nephilim").[9]
The use of these materials testifies to Rabbi Moshe's intellectual openness and to his being a guardian of ancient and rare traditions that seeped into the world of medieval midrash.[3, 9]
His Theological Teaching: The Messiah, the Light and the Redemption
Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan's midrashim are not merely textual exegesis; they carry within them profound conceptions of the structure of the world and the process of redemption. In "Bereshit Rabbati" and in the midrashim attributed to him there is a noticeable focus on the figure of the Messiah and on his spiritual supremacy.[10]
The Figure of the Messiah and the Hidden Light
Rabbi Moshe links the light created on the first day with the light of the Messiah. According to his view, the Messiah is a cosmic figure exalted not only above the patriarchs of the nation but even above the ministering angels.[10] His homilies on the verse "Behold, My servant shall prosper, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high" stress that the Messiah "shall be exalted above Abraham, and lifted up above Moses, and higher than the ministering angels."[10]
This conception of the Messiah as a primordial being located at the heart of creation gave his midrashim a messianic-apocalyptic dimension that was foreign to some of the later exegesis, but deeply influenced the esoteric teaching.[3, 10] The discussion of the struggle between the angels and the evil inclination, and of the power of holiness to survive within a material world, is a central theme of his homilies.[9]
Influence on Later Midrashim
Scholars identify the imprint of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan on a series of midrashim known as the late "Tanchuma-Yelammedenu midrashim":
Bamidbar Rabbah: large parts of the portions of Bamidbar and Naso are based directly on the midrashim of Rabbi Moshe.[3]
Devarim Rabbah: there is a Sephardic version of the midrash Devarim Rabbah quoted by Nahmanides (Ramban), whose editing scholars (such as Saul Lieberman) attribute to the circle of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan in Narbonne.[11]
His Public Work and His Disciples
Beyond his written work, Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan was a communal and educational leader. His yeshiva in Narbonne was a central institution that produced disciples who shaped the face of the Jewish world in the following generations. The most prominent of them was Rabbi Nathan ben Yechiel of Rome, who composed the "Arukh" in the second half of the 11th century.[1, 2] The fact that the author of the "Arukh" quotes Rabbi Moshe shows that the teaching of Rabbi Moshe was studied not only as biblical exegesis but as a foundation for understanding talmudic language and culture.[1, 2]
The leadership of the yeshiva by members of his family (his brother Levi and his son Yehuda) after his death ensured the continuity of the "School of Narbonne" for decades, and made the city a Torah center no less important than the centers in Babylonia or Ashkenaz at that time.[3]
Preservation and Historical Assessment
The legacy of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan is a legacy of bridges: a bridge between the Land of Israel and Europe, between the literature of the Second Temple and the Middle Ages, and between peshat and derash.[2, 12] Although his main work was lost, his presence in Rashi's commentary made him one of the sages who most influenced the shaping of the biblical consciousness of the Jewish people.[2]
Modern scholarship, from Avraham Epstein to Chanoch Albeck, restored to Rabbi Moshe his place as a brilliant editor and compiler, who knew how to preserve ancient traditions within a new exegetical world.[4, 5] The midrash "Bereshit Rabbati" serves today as a rare window onto the spiritual world of a sage who lived at a historical crossroads, and whose teaching continues to occupy scholars and students to this day.[4, 6]
In sum, Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan of Narbonne represents a type of Renaissance sage within the Torah world of the 11th century: a scholar, a preacher, an editor and, to some degree, a mystic, who laid the foundations ("Sefer Yesod") on which the edifice of the exegesis of the Rishonim was built.[1, 2] His extensive knowledge, stretching from the Second Temple period to his own days, makes him one of the most fascinating and significant figures in the history of Jewish thought.[2, 3]
